ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Withdrawal immediately after induction

A 32-year-old man dependent on a full opioid agonist takes buprenorphine before developing withdrawal from his previous opioid. Soon afterward he develops yawning, piloerection, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea. Which receptor property best explains this abrupt deterioration?

  1. Full mu-receptor agonism with greater intrinsic activity
  2. Irreversible destruction of mu receptors
  3. Selective activation of peripheral muscarinic receptors
  4. Increased metabolism of the prior opioid through enzyme induction
  5. High-affinity mu-receptor binding with partial agonist activity
Answer and explanation

High-affinity mu-receptor binding with partial agonist activity

Replacing a full agonist with buprenorphine can abruptly reduce receptor activation and precipitate withdrawal.

Option explanations

High-affinity mu-receptor binding with partial agonist activity: Replacing a full agonist with buprenorphine can abruptly reduce receptor activation and precipitate withdrawal.

Full mu-receptor agonism with greater intrinsic activity: Greater agonist activation would not explain this abrupt withdrawal.

Irreversible destruction of mu receptors: Buprenorphine does not destroy opioid receptors.

Selective activation of peripheral muscarinic receptors: This does not explain the opioid-dependent induction setting.

Increased metabolism of the prior opioid through enzyme induction: The immediate onset is better explained by receptor displacement.
